query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, elevated temperature combined with simultaneous mechanical wear and corrosive attack leads to rapid, cyclic formation and rupture of transient oxide films at the eutectic phase interfaces. This episodic oxide instability intermittently exposes chemically dissimilar phases that form local galvanic couples, thereby synergistically accelerating both wear and corrosion beyond the sum of their individual effects.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with refined intermetallic phases and matrix components whose wear and corrosion behaviors have been individually characterized.
generation.intervention: Introduce an in situ high-temperature tribocorrosion test that precisely controls oxygen partial pressure and mechanical load to modulate the stability and rupture frequency of the oxide films at phase interfaces.
generation.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to high mechanical load and a corrosive environment (e.g., chloride-containing solution or high oxygen activity atmosphere) at temperatures high enough to activate both rapid oxide film formation and accelerated diffusion at phase boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The eutectic phase interfaces between the intermetallic phases and the matrix, where transient oxide films form and rupture.
generation.mechanism: Mechanically induced rupture of newly formed protective oxide layers leads to repeated exposure of phase boundaries. The chemical potential differences between the exposed phases drive local galvanic corrosion, which in turn further destabilizes the oxide film. The interplay between wear-induced mechanical removal of oxides and galvanic corrosion accelerates overall material degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy with either isolated wear or corrosion conditions or with modified microstructure that minimizes phase potential differences, the alloy under simultaneous high-temperature tribocorrosion will exhibit a significantly higher total degradation rate, with both enhanced wear (from increased exposure of fresh surfaces) and accelerated corrosion (from stronger local galvanic effects).
generation.baseline: A matched alloy system where either the oxide film is stabilized (for example, through compositional modifications that reduce phase potential differences) or where wear and corrosion are applied independently under the same temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under sustained elevated temperature conditions that enable rapid oxide kinetics and under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive stresses. It may not apply at lower temperatures where oxide formation is more stable, or in systems with single-phase microstructures lacking interfacial galvanic couples.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of oxide rupture frequency versus galvanic coupling to accelerated degradation are uncertain, and platform-specific variations in microstructural details may alter the extent of synergy.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one with the standard multiphase microstructure and another engineered to minimize phase chemical potential differences (via compositional or processing modifications). Subject both sets to in situ high-temperature tribocorrosion testing while systematically varying oxygen partial pressure and mechanical load. Record the degradation responses as a function of these controlled variables.
measurements: Wear rate measurements via profilometry or microscopy
Corrosion current density by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or potentiodynamic polarization
Real-time monitoring of oxide film formation/rupture using in situ high-resolution microscopy or surface analysis techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled variations in oxygen partial pressure and mechanical load do not yield significant differences in total degradation, wear, and corrosion rates between the standard and modified alloys, or if degradation rates remain additive (i.e., the simultaneous exposure does not produce a synergistic effect), then the hypothesis that transient oxide instability coupled with galvanic effects drives accelerated degradation will be falsified.

AbstractThis work studies the fabrication of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding, addressing porosity and impurity issues in conventional methods. The HEA coatings exhibited eutectic/hypereutectic microstructures under all laser power conditions. A systematic investigation of laser power effects (1750–2500 W) reveals that 2250 W optimizes microstructure and performance, yielding a dual-phase structure with FCC matrix and dispersed σ phases (Fe-Cr/Mo-rich). The coating achieves exceptional hardness (738.3 HV0.2, 3.8× substrate), ultralow wear rate (4.55 × 10−5 mm3/N·m), and minimized corrosion current (2.31 × 10−4 A/cm2) in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. The friction mechanism of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating is that in high-speed friction and wear, the oxide film is formed on the surface of the coating, and then the rupture of the oxide film leads to adhesive wear and abrasive wear. The corrosion mechanism is the galvanic corrosion caused by the potential difference between the FCC phase and the σ phase.Keywords: high-entropy alloy coatings, coaxial powder-feeding laser cladding, CoCrFeNiMo, laser power

This study systematically investigates the microstructure evolution, tribological properties, and corrosion mechanisms of CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings fabricated via coaxial powder-fed laser cladding under variable laser power conditions. The key findings and implications are summarized as follows: The CoCrFeNiMo coatings exhibited a dual-phase structure comprising FCC and σ phases. At 2250 W, optimized energy density promoted homogeneous dispersion of Fe-Cr-rich σa and Fe-Mo-rich σb phases within the FCC matrix, forming a refined eutectic–hypereutectic hybrid microstructure. The hardness of the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coatings increased with laser power, peaking at 738.3 HV0.2 at 2250 W. This improvement was attributed to solution strengthening and second-phase intensification. However, at 2000 W, the hardness decreased due to grain coarsening caused by the extended molten pool duration. At a laser power of 2250 W, the CoCrFeNiMo HEA coating exhibited the lowest coefficient of friction (COF = 0.084) and excellent wear resistance. frame.system: A multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy, characterized by a complex microstructure with distinct intermetallic phases and matrix components, initially in a state where its individual wear and corrosion properties have been studied separately.
frame.goal: To propose a single mechanistic hypothesis that unifies the simultaneous wear and corrosion processes at elevated temperature, explaining why the coupled degradation is accelerated relative to a baseline where only one degradation mode or lower temperature conditions are present.
frame.limitation: Current understanding falls short in explaining the synergistic acceleration of degradation when wear and corrosion occur simultaneously at high temperatures, as opposed to the additive effects observed when these phenomena occur in isolation.

decision.trend: Early work established the concept of designing eutectic high-entropy alloys (PMC4145285) with alternating soft and hard phases to achieve superior mechanical properties at elevated temperatures. Later studies (PMC12156342, PMC12565319) began to examine wear and corrosion behaviors—often via laser cladding coatings—that revealed that degradation results from microstructural features unique to multiphase HEAs. In these works, researchers noted that under high-speed sliding, oxide films form then repeatedly break, leading to a mix of adhesive and abrasive wear; simultaneously, the phase-specific chemical potential differences set up local galvanic couples that accelerate corrosion. Although the wear and corrosion responses were quantified, the mechanistic connection between transient oxide film instability, phase interface dynamics, and accelerated degradation under simultaneous exposure remained only partially elucidated.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how the dynamic formation and rupture of protective oxide films at the eutectic phase interfaces couples with local galvanic effects under high temperature, mechanically demanding conditions. The unified mechanistic hypothesis that links wear-induced oxide film instability, interphase potential differences, and thermally accelerated diffusion processes has not been conclusively determined, particularly under truly coupled, in situ, high-temperature tribocorrosion conditions.
decision.lever: Implement an in situ high-temperature tribocorrosion test where environmental parameters such as oxygen partial pressure and mechanical load are precisely controlled to modulate the stability and rupture frequency of oxide films at the phase interfaces
decision.why: This approach directly builds on the observed trend where independent wear and corrosion tests provided clues—via oxide film formation/rupture and galvanic coupling—but did not isolate their synergistic interaction. By systematically varying key parameters in a controlled experiment while comparing against a matched baseline (e.g., alloys with minimized phase potential differences), one can effectively test whether transient oxide instability is the dominant mechanism behind accelerated coupled degradation under service-relevant, high-temperature conditions.
